title: How Small Law Firms and Solo Practitioners Can Harness Generative AI — full episode transcript
pub: AI and the Future of Law / 2030 Vision, American Arbitration Association
author: Jen Leonard · Bridget McCormack

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: The source materially develops the cluster’s proposed response by offering concrete AI-critical exercises: checking opinion summaries against the underlying judgment and using AI as a simulated appellate judge. Its evidence is practical and anecdotal, however, and it does not independently establish the broader claim that automation is eroding associate expertise reproduction.
qs: Ask it questions, ask it to summarize the opinion, see if you agree or disagree with the summary.

And then if you have extra time, pretend you’re preparing for an appellate argument about that case and ask the technology to serve in the role of a judge who’s challenging you on how this applies to your case.

st.t: Agentic delegation: Multistep work moves verification bottlenecks
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s core distinction between content generation and agentic delegation, and it recognizes materially different autonomy levels—from internet retrieval to authorized action. It does not address error propagation, verification bottlenecks, governance, or empirical reliability, so its support is conceptual and limited rather than an extension of the synthesis.
qs: Jen Leonard: And the other thing I was going to add onto your great definition of agentism is, you know, say your Gen AI produces a travel itinerary and instead of you having to then go on and make all the reservations, it would get your authorization and then go ahead and do those things for you.
So that is also agentism that already exists.

st.t: Continuous learning: Filtering matters more than release chasing
st.an: The source supports selective, contextual learning rather than exhaustive release chasing. McCormack recommends learning from faster-moving disciplines outside law, while Leonard acknowledges overload and expects platform-by-platform comparison to become less important as AI is embedded in existing practice software. These are practitioner recommendations and predictions, not empirical findings.
qs: And I’ve said this before as well, but I find that following people who are not necessarily in legal is quite useful with this technology, because it’s surprising to me how much there is to learn from other disciplines that are maybe diving into use cases a little faster, and it turns out they’re not necessarily that different from us.

But just to counter that or temper it a little bit, I would also say that I expect that this era where we’re all trying to find the different platforms in their most recent iterations—and which one compares to the others—will end at some point (or at least recede in its importance).

st.t: Court AI: Existing failures set the comparison
st.an: The source supports evaluating court AI as a practical response to unmet legal need rather than against an idealised system. It proposes multilingual public information and accessible preparation tools while carefully treating reported benefits as experiential or speculative, not demonstrated improvements in justice outcomes.
qs: Courts just never get through all the questions that they have from the public, and a public who, for the most part, can’t afford lawyers.
And yes, that example you’re recalling—I remember that lawyer saying that he can’t prove that ChatGPT helped him win oral argument, but he did win at oral argument.

st.t: Practitioner engagement: Redesign should precede technological certainty
st.an: The source aligns with the cluster’s practitioner-led emphasis on learning through everyday experimentation and broad organisational participation rather than waiting for technological certainty. It also reinforces the need for accessible, context-specific education for solo and small-firm practitioners, while offering only experiential—not comparative or outcome-based—evidence of benefits.
qs: So we thought it might be valuable to share some of the FAQs that we’re getting, and we’ll continue to do that in future episodes as well, because it’s probably a community that does not have as much access to some of the most cutting-edge technology or the conversations about it.
(Again, you heard from our conversation in the last episode that I’m a believer in pulling people from across your organization into using this technology.) And we’ve done that with HeyGen as well.

st.t: Professional engagement: Lawyers should shape AI deployment
st.an: The source supports the engagement-first proposition by promoting accessible AI education and continued learning for busy lawyers, especially solo and small-firm practitioners who may have less access to advanced technology and related discussions. Its contribution is limited to educational purpose and audience targeting; it provides no concrete implementation guidance or evidence of effectiveness.
qs: But we realized that many people in the day-to-day busyness of their lives don’t have the chance to really slow down and try to understand what the technology is, what its fundamental principles are, some helpful definitions and use cases.

So we thought it might be valuable to share some of the FAQs that we’re getting, and we’ll continue to do that in future episodes as well, because it’s probably a community that does not have as much access to some of the most cutting-edge technology or the conversations about it.

st.t: Selective augmentation: Verification constrains uneven productivity gains
st.an: The source endorses bounded, hands-on AI assistance for summarisation, appellate rehearsal and non-sensitive administrative work while requiring lawyers to compare outputs against their own judgment. Its effectiveness evidence is anecdotal rather than systematic, and it does not materially address verification burdens, junior development or staffing leverage.
qs: Ask it questions, ask it to summarize the opinion, see if you agree or disagree with the summary.

And then if you have extra time, pretend you’re preparing for an appellate argument about that case and ask the technology to serve in the role of a judge who’s challenging you on how this applies to your case.

st.t: Service redesign: Resistance reflects incentives and identity
st.an: The source supports treating AI adoption as more than product selection by emphasizing tailored education, an open mindset and purposeful experimentation. It applies that organisational-change logic to solo and small-firm practitioners, but offers practical guidance and predictions rather than evidence of completed service redesign or measured outcomes.
qs: That’s, I think, probably more important than figuring out which products are going to work for your practice.
Jen Leonard: And we’ve talked about tools and resources, but mindset is really key.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source supports selective, task-specific deployment by proposing bounded multilingual information and training uses rather than wholesale lawyer replacement. Its explicit limits on firsthand expertise and its largely speculative implementation claims also fit the synthesis’s caution that accessibility and plausible use cases do not establish reliable performance or realised outcomes.

kp.k: Small practices face distinct AI adoption barriers
kp.d: Leonard frames solo and small-firm practitioners as having less access to cutting-edge technology and related conversations than Big Law or legal-tech communities. Her reported audience questions reveal basic access and literacy needs, compounded by heavy workloads and the absence of internal IT training; these are practitioner observations rather than survey findings.
qs: The questions that I’ve been hearing are very different from the ones that I hear when I talk with people from Big Law or legal tech communities.
these were solo practitioners and small firms where there is not an IT team in-house thinking about these things or doing training on them.
Where do you actually access these things? Like, where is Claude? Where is ChatGPT?

kp.k: Prioritise affordable experimentation over legal-specific software
kp.d: McCormack recommends starting with browser-accessible general-purpose tools, available free or by subscription, reporting her own subscription as approximately $21.79 monthly. Leonard advises this audience against initially buying Harvey or CoCounsel on affordability grounds and recommends learning capabilities instead. Her expectation that prices will decline is a prediction, not established market evidence.
qs: you will be able to use it for free or buy a subscription (mine comes in at like $21.79 a month now, I feel like), which I highly recommend.
my first piece of advice is: don’t try to buy Harvey or CoCounsel.
I think the cost of all of these technologies will come down over time.
it’s less important to learn legal-specific technologies and more important to develop just a muscle for understanding what they can do currently.

kp.k: Experiment with public documents and human verification
kp.d: Leonard recommends reading and understanding a publicly available Supreme Court opinion before uploading it, then questioning the tool and checking its summary against the lawyer’s own understanding. She also recommends simulated judicial questioning and experimentation on non-sensitive administrative communications. Her assessment that summaries are increasingly accurate is personal experience, not a measured accuracy result.
qs: Read it yourself as a lawyer, understand it as a lawyer would, and then upload it to one of these platforms, and talk to it.
Ask it questions, ask it to summarize the opinion, see if you agree or disagree with the summary.
I find increasingly they’re pretty accurate, at least in summary.
ask the technology to serve in the role of a judge who’s challenging you on how this applies to your case.

kp.k: Keep early experimentation separate from sensitive information
kp.d: Leonard repeatedly limits suggested experiments to publicly available or non-sensitive material, including nonprivileged emails and marketing. In her personal translation example, she reports removing identifying information before uploading a screenshot. These are practical precautions articulated in the discussion, not an analysis of professional rules or a claim that any platform satisfies confidentiality requirements.
qs: I took a screenshot, but I was careful to eliminate any identifying data because I don’t want to ever put in anybody’s information.

for the administrative side of your work and the non-sensitive pieces of your work—like marketing or drafting an email to somebody that’s not privileged or confidential—find ways that you can adjust the tone to make it more diplomatic, to make it funnier.

kp.k: General-purpose tools can democratise appellate preparation
kp.d: McCormack recounts a small-firm or solo lawyer uploading public briefs, answering simulated appellate questions and requesting a decision to guide oral argument preparation. She reports that Paul Weiss partner Catherine Forrest uses the same approach, arguing that both practice settings can access the same tools. Leonard explicitly qualifies the successful-argument anecdote: the lawyer could not prove ChatGPT caused the win, although he found it useful for identifying additional questions.
qs: had the LLM ask him questions as if it were the appellate court.
And he answered the questions and had it write a decision.

you can be a solo practitioner in Pennsylvania doing an appellate argument before a state appellate court, or you can be Catherine Forrest preparing an argument for the Ninth Circuit, and you have access to the same tools.
he can’t prove that ChatGPT helped him win oral argument, but he did win at oral argument.

kp.k: Time savings may expand small-firm service capacity
kp.d: McCormack predicts that lawyers doing their own marketing and other operational work will quickly discover time savings from general-purpose AI. Leonard anticipates substantial potential to expand services and enter new markets. Neither speaker supplies quantified productivity, revenue or client-service evidence.
qs: you don’t have a marketing department or an IS department—but you will quickly see how much time these tools save you.
for solos and smalls the transformative power is huge; the ability to grow the service you provide, to open up new markets for you, is enormous

kp.k: Video generation lowers specialist production barriers
kp.d: McCormack reports that her team uses HeyGen for internal training and public-facing service information despite lacking video-production experience. A staff member is developing a video explaining consistent data entry to case managers, illustrating AI-supported operational training and preparation for future data uses. McCormack reports positive translation feedback from colleagues but expressly says she has not assessed translations herself.
qs: none of them are at all experienced in video creation.
it’s really incredible how it can turn a text script into a video.
she’s working on making a video to explain to staff (case managers, for entering data) why it’s important to enter it in a particular way.
I haven’t, and I would not be the person to be able to assess the translation frankly.

kp.k: Multilingual court information could scale public assistance
kp.d: McCormack proposes AI-generated multilingual videos as a way for courts and firms to move beyond one-to-one information provision. She links the court application to unanswered public questions and people unable to afford lawyers. Leonard imagines procedural FAQs delivered through courthouse kiosks or websites, while McCormack prefers reaching people before they need to attend court. These are prospective access-to-justice applications, not reported deployments or measured outcomes.
qs: Courts just never get through all the questions that they have from the public, and a public who, for the most part, can’t afford lawyers.

You could imagine firms being able to provide information about the kinds of things they can do, not in the one-to-one service model that we’re all used to, and therefore reach far more people than we can reach right now.
If courts put it on their websites and figure out a way to, like, get that information into people’s hands before they have to come to court, even better, right?

kp.k: Generated videos could support differentiated legal education
kp.d: Leonard envisages asynchronous law-student content and differentiated training for varied learner preferences. McCormack reports that her education team finds video generation more user-friendly and predicts easier creation of individualised learning modules. The discussion does not establish improvements in learning outcomes.
qs: I could imagine educational and training offerings that meet different populations of learners in a way that they really prefer by having different videos present to them.
Our education team is playing with it and they think it’s so much more user-friendly for the video content that they’re creating.
it’s also going to be a lot easier to put together individualized learning modules.

kp.k: Agentic systems shift from answering to performing tasks
kp.d: McCormack describes agentic AI as partly autonomous, goal-oriented activity rather than simply responding to questions, and expects its importance to increase in coming months and years. Leonard illustrates the concept with an itinerary tool obtaining authorisation and making reservations. She also characterises internet retrieval as existing agentism while distinguishing retrieved current information from the model’s training cutoff; these are the speakers’ explanatory claims rather than demonstrated legal workflows.
qs: it’s not just responding to your question (which is something that probably everybody by now has had an experience with AIs doing), but actively seeking to get something done for you, like a task or a goal
instead of you having to then go on and make all the reservations, it would get your authorization and then go ahead and do those things for you.
But that doesn’t mean its training is current, if that makes sense. It’s going to get new information and fold it into its response.

kp.k: Unstructured information becomes a resource for legal AI
kp.d: Leonard presents the ability to query documents and text-heavy files and derive predictive outcomes as a potential breakthrough for law. McCormack contrasts predefined spreadsheet and database formats with emails, recordings and social-media posts, arguing that generative AI makes the latter valuable. These are conceptual explanations of the proposed mechanism, not evidence of predictive performance.
qs: One of the reasons that Gen AI could be such a breakthrough is that we can actually use that unstructured data now to make predictive outcomes from it or ask it questions and talk to it
I think of structured data as data that’s organized in a predefined format.
I think of unstructured data as—you know—emails and audio recordings and social media posts and the ways in which we live our lives in words, either in writing or in speaking.

kp.k: Learning networks and experimentation support continuing adaptation
kp.d: Leonard recommends local bar education and social-media learning, naming Bob Ambrogi and Niki Shaver. McCormack recommends Jordan Furlong, Paul Roetzer, Mike Kaput and Ethan Mollick, stressing learning from disciplines outside law. Both favour an open, experimental mindset; McCormack’s suggestion that this will yield more satisfying and probably more successful practices is a forecast.
qs: I would start with my local bar association and see what conversations are happening and if there are any educational resources available.
I actually think social media is a much better way to learn about this tech than, you know, waiting for the next edition of whatever legal resource you consume periodically.
there is to learn from other disciplines that are maybe diving into use cases a little faster
people who have a growth mindset right now are the ones who are going to have a more satisfying and probably more successful practice tomorrow.

kp.k: Embedded AI may reduce platform-selection burdens
kp.d: Leonard predicts that constantly tracking competing platforms will become less important as AI is integrated into software practitioners already use. McCormack similarly expects products to settle out. Their recommendation is to understand possibilities without trying to master every product or immediately determine the best legal-specific purchase; no firm adoption timetable is supplied.
qs: a lot of this technology will become infused and integrated into the tech that you’re already using in your practice.
I wouldn’t necessarily try to boil the ocean and learn everything you can about generative AI, because I think it will arrive to you in a more consumable way sooner than later.
I would be learning as much as you can about what the possibilities are.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Leonard and McCormack describe accessible generative AI as a means of saving small-practice time, supporting legal preparation, expanding service reach and making information and training easier to produce.
pts.d: McCormack claims that solos and small firms will quickly discover time savings, including where lawyers perform administrative functions themselves. Leonard describes increasingly accurate opinion summaries and proposes lawyer-checked summarisation, simulated appellate questioning and non-sensitive administrative drafting as starting uses. McCormack argues that general-purpose tools give solos and elite-firm lawyers access to the same argument-preparation capabilities. Leonard predicts declining technology costs, integration into existing practice software and substantial opportunities for small practices to expand services and enter new markets. McCormack and Leonard envisage multilingual video enabling courts and firms to reach more people than one-to-one information provision permits; they also anticipate easier differentiated and individualised training. Leonard claims generative AI makes unstructured material usable for questions and predictions. McCormack expects autonomous, goal-directed AI to become a more prominent topic and predicts that practitioners with a growth mindset will have more satisfying and probably more successful practices. These are the speakers' own claims and forecasts, not established outcomes.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence consists primarily of personal experience, organisational experimentation and reported practitioner anecdotes; no quantified legal-performance or market evidence is supplied.
pts.d: McCormack reports that her organisation's inexperienced video creators are using HeyGen for training and service information, and that the education team finds it user-friendly. Translation quality is reported by team members, not assessed personally by McCormack. Leonard's assessment of legal summaries rests on her own use. The speakers recount an unnamed practitioner's report that simulated appellate questioning helped preparation; Leonard explicitly preserves his inability to establish that ChatGPT caused his courtroom success. McCormack also invokes Catherine Forrest's use of similar preparation techniques as a practitioner example, rather than comparative performance evidence. Leonard's separate German-text translation anecdote involves confirmation by her German-speaking friend, not a legal translation evaluation. Price declines, integration, new markets, public-service transformation and improved practice success are forecasts without supporting datasets or benchmarks in this transcript.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The 2024 discussion distinguishes immediately available experimentation from loosely timed forecasts, while qualifying recommended legal uses by public-data selection and human checking.
pts.d: Time savings, general-purpose access, summarisation, simulated argument preparation and organisational video creation are presented as available now. Leonard recommends starting with a publicly available opinion that the lawyer has already read and understood, then checking agreement with its AI summary; her administrative examples exclude privileged or confidential material. The reported appellate simulation likewise used publicly available filings. This is lawyer-in-the-loop assistance, not a recommendation to rely directly on autonomous legal output. Legal-specific tools are described as currently having affordability barriers for the target audience; anticipated price reductions occur 'over time,' without a date. Integration is expected 'sooner than later,' with platform comparison eventually ending or becoming less important. Public-facing court benefits depend on administrators implementing accessible videos, kiosks or websites and getting information to users. Individualised training is prospective. McCormack expects increased discussion of agentic systems over the coming months and years, not a dated commitment to autonomous legal-service deployment. Her practice-success prediction is conditional on a growth mindset and expressed probabilistically.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal beneficiaries envisaged are resource-constrained solos and small firms, court users without lawyers, multilingual audiences and learners with differing needs.
pts.d: For solos and small firms without in-house IT, marketing or training resources, the speakers anticipate accessible experimentation, reduced administrative effort, enhanced preparation and potential service expansion. Large-firm lawyers provide a comparison: specialist products may remain differently affordable, but some general-purpose capabilities are shared. Courts and court administrators could scale procedural and service information rather than answer every question individually. The access-to-justice claim concerns members of the public who cannot afford lawyers, including self-represented litigants and people needing information in their native language; websites may help them before they travel to court, while kiosks assist those already there. Firms could also reach more prospective users through service-information videos. Organisational staff, case managers, education teams, lawyers, judges and law students are discussed as creators or recipients of more accessible and tailored training.
